sec.title: Background
sec.p: HH2853 is a novel dual EZH1/2 inhibitor that exhibits superior antitumour activity compared to tazemetostat across various preclinical models. Here, we evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and preliminary efficacy of HH2853 in patients with refractory advanced solid tumours and non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs).

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This open-label, global multicentre, phase I study was conducted at 12 centres in China and the USA, enrolling patients (aged ≥18 years) with relapsed or refractory solid tumours or NHLs. For dose escalation, seven predefined dose levels of HH2853 (50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 mg, orally twice daily for 28 days) were evaluated using a standard Bayesian optimal interval with accelerated titration design. Two dose levels were selected for dose extension. Primary endpoints were safety, dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and recommended phase II dose (RP2D). Secondary and exploratory endpoints included PK/PD profiles and preliminary efficacy. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04390737.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: Between Sept 8, 2020, and Feb 28, 2023, 61 patients received HH2853. As of Jan 5, 2024, the median follow-up was 15.7 months (interquartile range [IQR], 13.8–17.7). Two DLTs were observed in patients at 800 mg dose level. MTD was not reached. The dose levels of 400 mg and 600 mg were selected for dose extension, and the RP2D was determined as 400 mg twice daily. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of any grade occurred in 58 patients (95.1%). The most common TRAEs were diarrhoea (n = 31, 50.8%), blood bilirubin increased (n = 29, 47.5%) and anaemia (n = 23, 37.7%). The most common TRAEs of grade ≥3 included anaemia (n = 7, 11.5%), diarrhoea (n = 5, 8.2%), and platelet count decreased (n = 4, 6.6%). No treatment-related deaths were reported. Among 57 efficacy-evaluable patients, 17 (27.9%) achieved an objective response, with four complete responses and 13 partial responses. Ten of 17 objective responses (58.8%) were observed in patients with epithelioid sarcoma (ES). The objective response rate in patients with ES was 31.3% (95% confidence interval [CI], 16.0–50.0), and the median progression-free survival was 16.0 months (95% CI, 5.2–19.1).

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: HH2853 showed a manageable safety profile and encouraging antitumour activity in refractory solid tumours and NHLs, with particularly promising antitumour activity in ES. Further trials are needed. A phase II trial of HH2853 in patients with ES is underway.

sec.title: Evidence before this study
sec.p: We searched PubMed in English from database inception to Dec 18, 2024 for clinical trials that reported inhibitors targeting enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH) or in patients with cancer. Search terms included (“EZH2” OR “EZH1”) AND “cancer” and filtered for clinical trial. The search yielded 44 entries, of which 18 were studies of EZH1/2 or EHZ2 inhibitors as monotherapy or combination therapy, including EZH1/2 inhibitor valemetostat and EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat, GSK2816126, and SHR2554.11 studies were for EZH1 inhibitors or EZH1/2 inhibitors. Four phase I studies of tazemetostat demonstrated acceptable safety and preliminary antitumour activity in relapsed/refractory (R/R) B-cell lymphomas and advanced solid tumours, both as monotherapy and in combination. SHR2554 showed similar safety and activity in two phase I trials for R/R mature lymphoid neoplasms. GSK2816126 (n = 20) was tolerable at 2400 mg twice daily but had limited efficacy in R/R B-cell lymphomas. Valemetostat monotherapy (n = 90) exhibited favourable safety and clinical activity in R/R non-Hodgkin lymphoma, while its combination with irinotecan (n = 22) was poorly tolerated but showed some efficacy in recurrent small-cell lung cancer. Among six phase II studies, four evaluated tazemetostat: 1) In advanced BAF47/SMARCB1-deficient epithelioid sarcoma (n = 62), with encouraged safety profile and efficacy; 2) In R/R follicular lymphoma (n = 99), responses were durable, with higher objective response rates in EZH2-mutated vs. wild-type cases; 3) A Japanese trial (n = 20) confirmed efficacy in EZH2-mutated R/R B-cell lymphomas; 4) In BAP1-inactivated malignant pleural mesothelioma (n = 74), preliminary activity was observed, though biomarker refinement is needed to optimize patient selection. Another 2 phase II studies assessed valemetostat, demonstrating promising efficacy and tolerability in heavily pretreated R/R adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma and peripheral T-cell lymphoma.

sec.title: Added value of this study
sec.p: This phase I study assessed HH2853, a novel orally EZH1/2 dual inhibitor, across relapsed/refractory non-Hodgkin lymphomas or advanced solid tumours. HH2853 at 400 mg twice daily had acceptable safety profile. This study reports promising antitumour activity of an EZH1/2 dual inhibitor-HH2853 in relapsed/refractory non-Hodgkin's lymphomas and advanced solid tumours, particularly in epithelioid sarcoma.

sec.title: Implications of all the available evidence
sec.p: Our data supports the further exploration of HH2853 in patients with epithelioid sarcoma, which has the potential to improve current therapeutic practice. Our findings, coupled with previously published studies suggest that a dual inhibition of EZH1/2 is also a potential therapeutic strategy and that it has the potential to be more effective than EZH2-only inhibitors. Future research should focus on larger-scale randomised controlled trials to validate these results and identify patients with epithelioid sarcoma that may benefit from this treatment.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) act as an epigenetic regulator, playing a crucial role in cancer cell proliferation, differentiation and metastasis by mediating gene silencing through trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me3). PRC2 function is frequently deregulated in cancer, positioning it as a promising candidate for therapeutic target.1 The core subunits of PRC2 include enhancer of zeste homolog 1/2 (EZH1/2), embryonic ectoderm development (EED), suppressor of zeste 12 (SUZ12), and RBBP4/7.2 EZH2 serve as the main catalytic subunit, exerting a decisive impact on PRC2 activity.3 EZH2 is often overexpressed or mutated in malignancies like follicular lymphoma (FL), prostate carcinoma, and soft-tissue sarcoma, leading to repression of tumour suppressor genes.4, 5, 6, 7 additionally, switch/sucrose nonfermenting (SWI/SNF) complex, an ATP-dependent remodeller, functions as a tumour suppressor. SWI/SNF and PRC2 complexes exhibit a mutually antagonistic relationship, with SWI/SNF often counteracting PRC2-mediated gene silencing.8 SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex is composed of SWI/SNF related matrix associated actin dependent regulator of chromatin A subfamily member 4 (SMARCA4)/(BRG)1, SWI/SNF related matrix associated actin dependent regulator of chromatin B subfamily member 1 (SMARCB1)/BAF47, and AT-rich interaction domain 1A (ARID1A). Loss-of-function mutations in these subunits can contribute to the dysfunction of SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex.9 Genomic studies have revealed that cancers like sarcoma and undifferentiated tumours frequently harbour mutations in either SWI/SNF or PRC2, but rarely both, often indicating worse anti-tumour responses and prognosis.10, 11, 12, 13 SWI/SNF-deficient tumours often depend on EZH2 activity, making them susceptible to EZH2 inhibitors.14,15 Thus, EZH2 represents a potential therapeutic target in cancer treatment.

Currently, several EZH2 inhibitors are being evaluated in clinical studies for non-Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) and advanced solid tumours.16,17 Tazemetostat and SHR2554, both EZH2 inhibitors, have demonstrated anti-tumour activity in patients with metastatic/locally advanced epithelioid sarcoma (ES) and/or several lymphomas.18, 19, 20, 21 However, the objective response rate (ORR) of EZH2 inhibitor (tazemetostat) is approximately 15% with a progression-free survival (PFS) of 5.5 months in advanced ES.20 In lymphomas, EZH2 inhibitors achieve an ORR of 45–60% with a median PFS of 12–14 months,18,21 indicating limited efficacy and survival benefit. Reported studies have shown that EZH1 plays a complementary yet distinct role from EZH2, retaining partial catalytic function even in the absence of core PRC2 components. This suggests a more stable role in maintaining long-term gene silencing.22 Inhibitors targeting both EZH1 and EZH2 may potentially exhibit superior efficacy compared to single EZH2 inhibitors, given the reciprocal interference and compensatory mechanisms between EZH1 and EZH2.

HH2853 is a novel, potent, and selective small molecule inhibitor targeting EZH1/2. Preclinical studies have shown that HH2853 exhibited higher anti-tumour activity in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, peripheral T-cell lymphoma, and various solid tumour models with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex alterations.23,24 While valemetostat, a dual EZH1/2 inhibitor, was approved by the FDA in patients with refractory adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphomaand demonstrated preliminary efficacy in relapsed or refractory NHLs,25, 26, 27 limited data exist on the efficacy of dual EZH1/2 inhibitors in other advanced solid tumours, particularly ES.

Thus, we designed a phase I/II study to evaluate the safety, pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and preliminary antitumour activity of HH2853 in patients with advanced solid tumours and relapsed/refractory NHLs.

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice guidelines. The trial protocol is available as appendix 1. All versions of study protocols were approved by the ethics committee of each centre. The specific names of the authorities that granted ethical approval for the study are available in the Supplementary Material, Table S1. All eligible patients provided written informed consent prior to study enrolment.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This is an open-label, global multicentre, single-arm, phase I/II study comprising three parts: (1) a dose escalation phase I study, (2) a dose extension phase I study in advanced solid tumours and NHL, and (3) a phase II study at recommended phase II dose (RP2D) in selective tumours. Here, we report the results from the dose escalation and extension parts of phase I study. All patients were enrolled at 12 centres in China and the US. Details on the 12 centres are given in the Supplementary Material (Table S2), including site name, location, type, and number of participants recruited. This study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04390737).

In the dose escalation part, a standard Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN)28 with accelerated titration (ATD) design was adopted to guide toxicity monitoring and dose escalation. Seven dose-level cohorts, 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg, 400 mg, 600 mg, 800 mg, and 1000 mg twice daily in a continuous 28-day treatment cycle, were designed to dose escalation (Supplementary Material, Figure S1). In the ATD part in the dose-escalation phase, one patient per cohort received HH2853: orally once daily on day 1 to evaluate single-dose PKs, then twice daily from day 2 onward. If a grade ≥2 adverse event (AE) occurred, the dose escalation switched to a standard BOIN design, in which at least three patients per treatment cohort were enrolled. HH2853 was administered twice daily to assess the dose-limiting toxicity (DLT). The acceptable toxicity probability interval of target DLT was set as 0.25 (0.197, 0.298). Thirty-one patients were enrolled for the dose escalation part.

Two selected dose levels were extended to collect more safety, PK, PD, and preliminary antitumour activity data to determine RP2D. Thirty-one patients were enrolled in the dose extension part and received continuous HH2853 twice daily.

Eligible patients included those with relapsed or refractory NHLs who had received at least two prior systemic treatment regimens, or those with advanced solid tumours that had either progressed, were intolerant to standard therapies, or had no available standard treatment options. The escalation phase had no mutational requirements. For the dose extension part, patients with relapsed/refractory NHL, ES, or other advanced solid tumours with specific loss-of-function genetic alterations in PRC2 or SWI/SNF complex components were included, such as mutations or deficiencies in EZH2, SMARCA4/BRG1, ARID1A, SMARCB1/BAF47, or BRCA1-associated protein 1 (BAP1), detected by next-generation sequencing (NGS) or immunohistochemistry (IHC).

In both the dose escalation and extension phases, patients were eligible for if they were ages of 18 years or older, had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1, a life expectancy of at least three months and adequate organ functions. Patients enrolled in dose extension part required at least one measurable lesion per the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) version 1.1 for solid tumours or Lugano 2014 for lymphomas and had to provide archival tissue within three years for exploratory biomarker studies.

Data were collected on previous therapies (systemic therapy, radiotherapy, surgery). The minimum washout period was 28 days or five half-lives (whichever was shorter) from prior chemotherapy, immunotherapy and target therapies, and 14 days for previous palliative local site radiotherapy. Exclusions included symptomatic central nervous system metastases, major surgery within 4 weeks, active infection and HIV infection, history of other malignancies before enrolment, and gastrointestinal disorders that would prevent drug absorption. Progression (not defined by RECIST version 1.1) before study entry was determined by the treating physician. Additional inclusion/exclusion criteria are detailed in the study protocols.

sec.title: Randomisation and masking
sec.p: This was an open-label study; therefore, no blinding or masking of investigators or participants occurred. Similarly, this single-arm study did not involve randomisation.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: HH2853 was administered orally twice daily in a fasted state, or at least 1 h before or 2 h after a meal. Patients continued to fast for 1 h after the administration of each HH2853 dose. Patients had the HH2853 in continuous 28 days until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, patients requestion, consent withdrawal, or study termination, whichever occurred first. Dose modification was not permitted in DLT observation period. Outside of DLT observation, dose interruptions and reductions were allowed as per protocol. Typically, Grade 1–2 AEs did not require dose modifications. And no more than two dose modifications were permitted.

Safety was assessed in both the dose escalation and extension phases of the phase I study. All AEs were recorded and categorized by severity (National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events [NCI-CTCAE] version 5.0) and relationship to HH2853. The treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) included all AEs considered probably and definitely related to the study drugs. After treatment completion, participants were followed up for AEs for 28 days from the last HH2853 dose. The DLT was evaluated in all patients who received at least 80% of the planned dose during the phase I dose escalation. A DLT was defined as a TRAE (determined by the investigator and/or sponsor) occurring within 28 days after the first dose, meeting the predefined criteria per NCI-CTCAE version 5.0. DLTs were defined as follows: any grade ≥4 hematologic toxicities (except for grade 4 neutropenia and anaemia lasting ≤7 days), grade 3 thrombocytopenia lasting >7 days or requiring platelet transfusion, febrile neutropenia, any grade ≥3 cardiac event or corrected QT Interval (QTc) prolongation, grade ≥3 non-hematologic toxicities (except for grade 3 single abnormality in the laboratory test, grade 3 fatigue and prolonged corrected QT interval ≤3 days, grade 3 diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting ≤5 days after supportive treatment, grade 3 elevated ALT/AST ≤7 days), or any other grade 3 contributed to drug interruption for over seven days. And any grade ≥2 non-hematologic toxicities contribute to drug delay for more than 2 weeks.

Clinical response was evaluated by investigators per RECIST v1.1 for solid tumours or Lugano 2014 for lymphomas at baseline, every 8 weeks (±7 days) for 48 weeks post-first dose, then every 12 weeks (±7 days) until disease progression, new antitumour therapy initiation, consent withdrawal, loss to follow-up, or study completion. All partial response cases were confirmed after ≥4 weeks. Efficacy was assessed by both investigators and qualified imaging physician. Patients with clinical benefit could continue HH2853 beyond RECIST-defined progression at the investigator's discretion.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: Primary safety endpoints were AE incidence, type, and severity (assessed according to NCI-CTCAE version 5.0), and tolerability; primary efficacy endpoints were maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and RP2D. Secondary endpoints evaluated the plasma concentration–time profiles and derived PK parameters of HH2853 and potential metabolites. Exploratory endpoints included the preliminary efficacy including ORR, duration of response (DoR), PFS, disease control rate (DCR), time to response (TTR), and overall survival (OS), PD analysis, and the biomarker analysis.

sec.title: PK and PD analysis
sec.p: Blood samples for HH2853 PK evaluation were collected at (1) during the single dose phase: cycle 1 day 1 (C1D1) at pre-dose, and 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 (optional), and 24 h post-dose; (2) after multiple doses on day 15 (C1D15) at pre-dose and 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 (optional), and 24 h post-dose; on cycle 2 day 1 and day 15 (pre-dose); on cycle 3 day 1 and cycle 4 day 1 (pre-dose). Plasma concentrations of HH2853 were analysed using a liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry assay (Shimadzu Corporation, LC-30AD), with a lower limit of quantification of 2.585 ng/mL for HH2853. PK parameters were calculated for HH2853 concentration–time data using the Phoenix Winnonlin software version 8.3: Cmax, Tmax, Ctrough (pre-dose concentration), AUC0–12 (area under the plasma concentration–time curve from time 0 to 12 h), Cavg0–12 (mean plasma concentration from 0 to 12 h), t1/2, CLss/F (apparent clearance in plasma at steady state), and AR (accumulation ratios).

For PD analysis, H3K27me3 level in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was measured by flow cytometry. The inhibitory effect of HH2853 on H3K27me3 was evaluated by measuring the mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of H3K27me3 and total H3 in peripheral monocytes, then calculating the relative expression level of H3K27me3 (MFI: H3K27me3/H3). Whole-blood samples for PBMCs were collected on C1D1 at pre-dose, and on C1D15 at post-dose 8 h.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: This was a phase I exploratory trial. No formal statistical hypotheses were pre-specified. The sample size was not determined on the basis of a statistical hypothesis. The phase I part of the study enrolled 61 patients. To reliably estimate the MTD, 31 patients evaluable for the observation of DLT were enrolled in the dose escalation phase. Two dose levels were selected for dose extension with approximately 15 patients per cohort. There was no formal interim analysis in this study. The safety analysis was based on the safety analysis set including all study patients who received at least one dose of the study drug. The PK analysis was based on a PK analysis set including patients who received at least one dose of the study drug and had valid PK samples to estimate key parameters for at least one of the days of sampling. The PD analysis was based on a PD analysis set including patients who received at least one dose of the study drug and had valid PD samples to estimate key parameters. The response results were summarized based on the response evaluable analysis set including all patients who received at least one dose of the study drug and tumour assessment during treatment. Patients baseline characteristics were summarized by descriptive statistics. The Kaplan–Meier method was used to summarize time-to-event endpoints, and 95% CIs for the medians were calculated using the Brookmeyer-Crowley method. ORR and DCR were summarized using a point estimate and 95% Clopper-Pearson confidence interval (CI). Subgroup efficacy analyses were performed for the ES, FL and other tumour subgroup. All the analyses were prespecified in protocol or statistical analysis plan. R (version 4.2.1) was used for statistical analysis of the experiments, data processing and presentation.

sec.title: Role of the funding source
sec.p: The funder and authors were all involved in study design; data collection, data analyses, data interpretation, and manuscript preparation and submission. The funder had full access to the dataset. All authors verified that this study was performed according to the protocol and attested to the accuracy and completeness of the data. The corresponding authors had final responsibility for the decision to submit for publication.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Between Sept 8, 2020, and Feb 28, 2023, 87 patients were screened, and 61 patients were finally enrolled in the phase I study (dose escalation part, n = 31; dose extension part, n = 30) and treated with HH2853 (Fig. 1). At the data cut-off on January 5, 2024, the median follow-up duration was 15.7 months (interquartile range [IQR], 13.8–17.7). 15 patients (26.4%) remained on treatment with HH2853, while 46 patients (75.4%) dropping out of study for disease progression (n = 38), patients request (n = 5), AEs (n = 2), or death (n = 1) (Fig. 1). The death was due to a cerebrovascular accident and occurred 434 days after treatment initiation, and the investigator determined this event to be unrelated to the study drug.

sec.p: Baseline demographic characteristics are shown in Table 1. Among enrolled patients, 33 (54.1%) were males, and 28 (45.9%) had a median age of 43 years (range: 20–82). 32 patients (52.5%) had ES, seven patients (11.5%) had FL, and 22 patients (36.1%) had other solid tumours. The majority were of Asian ethnicity (n = 44, 72.1%), followed by White (n = 16, 26.2%) and Black or African American (n = 1, 1.6%). Patients had undergone extensive pretreatment, with 44.3% (n = 27) having received at least three lines of prior systemic antitumour therapy, and all patients with ES had received prior treatment. 39 (63.9%) patients had at least one mutation in EZH2, SMARCB1, SMARCA4, ARID1A, or BAP1, or loss of BAF47 expression (Table 1). EZH2 mutation status was available for one (1.6%) patient with FL (Y646F). BAF47 was negative in 34 (55.7%) patients by IHC, including 31 with ES, one with epithelioid angiosarcoma (the root of the perineal thigh), one with malignant tumour of the nasal cavity, and one with an unspecified BAF47-negative tumour. Two patients (3.3%) harbored SMARCA4 genetic alterations, including one with thoracic SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumour (immunohistochemically negative for SMARCA4) and another with high-grade pleural sarcoma carrying a canonical splice site mutation (c.2974-2A > T). One patient with endometrial carcinoma harbored heterozygous ARID1A mutation (p.E1542∗ exon18; p.K2146Vfs∗3 exon20). One patient with mesothelioma harbored heterozygous BAP1 mutation (p.D184V exon 7).

sec.p: All enrolled patients who received at least one dose of HH2853 were included in the safety analysis. At the data cutoff (Jan 5, 2024), the median exposure to HH2853 was 7.8 months (IQR, 1.8–15.2).

In dose escalation part, 31 patients were distributed in six dose-level cohorts (50 mg, n = 1; 100 mg, n = 1; 200 mg n = 3; 400 mg, n = 4; 600 mg n = 13; 800 mg, n = 9). The dose escalation process is summarized in Supplementary Material, Table S3. 29 patients completed DLT observation, while two patients (400 mg, n = 1; 800 mg, n = 1) did not finish due to patient request. Two DLTs were observed at dose level of 800 mg, including a grade 3 platelet count decreased lasting 9 days (meeting DLT criteria of grade 3 thrombocytopenia lasting >7 days) and a grade 3 diarrhoea lasting 6 days (meeting DLT criteria of grade 3 thrombocytopenia lasting ≥5 days). The MTD was not reached per study design. But the 1000 mg dose was terminated for safety consideration after discussion between investigators and sponsor. Based on the safety analysis, the dose levels of 400 mg and 600 mg twice daily were selected for dose extension.

The safety profile is summarized in Table 2 and Supplementary Material, Table S4. 58 patients (95.1%) experienced at least one TRAE of any grade, and 24 patients (39.3%) experienced TRAEs of grade 3 or above. The most common TRAEs were diarrhoea (n = 31, 50.8%), blood bilirubin increased (n = 29, 47.5%) and anaemia (n = 23, 37.7%). The most common TRAEs of grade 3 or above included anaemia (n = 7, 11.5%), diarrhoea (n = 5, 8.2%), and platelet count decreased (n = 4, 6.6%). Treatment-related serious adverse events (SAEs) occurred in four patients (6.6%), with anaemia (n = 3, 4.9%) being the most common. No patient died from TRAEs. One death due to a cerebrovascular accident (400 mg BID group) was unrelated to HH2853, as determined by the investigator and sponsor (related to the participant's history of deep vein thrombosis and hypercoagulable state). One patient (1.6%) discontinued due to TRAE (anaemia). Treatment interruption occurred in 19 patients (31.1%) with the most common TRAEs including blood bilirubin increased (n = 5, 8.2%), anaemia (n = 4, 6.6%), platelet count decreased (n = 3, 4.9%), aspartate aminotransferase increased (n = 2, 3.3%), and white blood cell count decreased (n = 2, 3.3%). The median durations of interruptions caused by these AEs ranged from 2 to 8 days. Treatment reduction occurred in 11 patients (18.0%) for TRAEs with the most common TRAEs including platelet count decreased (n = 3, 4.9%), anaemia (n = 2, 3.3%), hypokalaemia (n = 2, 3.3%), neutrophil count decreased (n = 2, 3.3%).

sec.p: 59 of 61 patients across six dose-level cohorts were available for PK analysis (detailed in Supplementary Material, Table S5). After single and multiple oral dose administration, HH2853 plasma concentration–time profiles increased with dose (Fig. 2a and b). HH2853 was rapidly absorbed with a median Tmax of 0.5–2.0 hous, with no apparent dose-dependence. The mean half-life (t1/2) of HH2853 was 1–4 h. Exposure showed a relatively dose-related increase over 50–600 mg BID, with high inter-participant variation. Exposure at 800 mg was lower than expected. No racial differences were found, and PK characteristics in solid tumours were similar to other patients (Supplementary Material, Table S6 and Figure S2a and b).

sec.p: 53 patients were available for PD analysis. HH2853 demonstrated target (EZH1/2) engagement by inhibiting of H3K27me3 in peripheral monocytes. Dose- and exposure-dependent inhibition of H3K27me3 was observed at 200–600 mg. At both 400 mg and 600 mg, HH2853 showed robust H3K27me3 inhibition (median inhibition rate of over 50%), with no significant difference in inhibition occurred in both overall population and patients with solid tumours (Fig. 2c, Supplementary Material, Figure S2c).

At the cut-off date of Jan 5, 2024, 57 patients completed efficacy evaluation, while another four patients dropping out before the first evaluation for patients request (n = 3) and clinical disease progression (n = 1). The efficacy across dose levels is summarized in Supplementary Material, Table S7. Among evaluable patients, 17 patients had objective response including ES (n = 10), FL (n = 5), one with an unspecified BAF47-negative tumour (n = 1) and malignant rhabdoid tumour with SMARCB1 mutation (n = 1). Four patients achieved complete response (CR): 400 mg (n = 2), 600 mg (n = 1) and 800 mg (n = 1); 13 patients achieved partial response (PR): 200 mg (n = 1), 400 mg (n = 3), 600 mg (n = 7) and 800 mg (n = 2). The overall ORR was 29.8% (95% CI, 18.4–43.4) with eight (47%) responses; 15 of 17 responders (88.2%) were in 400 mg or above. In addition, 24 patients had stable disease (SD), yielding an overall DCR of 71.9% (95% CI, 58.5–83.0). The median PFS was 9.0 months (95% CI, 3.7–16.0).

Among 32 evaluable patients with ES, the ORR was 31.3% (95% CI, 16.0–50.0), with 26 having SD and a DCR of 81.3% (64.0–93.0). The median TTR was 3.0 months (IQR, 2.0–4.1), median PFS was 16.0 months (95% CI, 5.2–19.1), and median OS was not reached (Table 3). Seven of 10 patients with PR continued HH2853. One patient who achieved CR at week 24 had a 19.5-month response ongoing at data cut-off (Fig. 3, Supplementary Material, Figure S4).

sec.p: Four of six patients with FL (66.7%; 95% CI, 22.3–95.7) had objective responses, including three CRs and one PR. Two CRs were confirmed by negative 18F-FDG-PET (Supplementary Material, Figure S3). The EZH2-mutated (Y646F) patient achieved a durable CR with a DoR of 12.6 months.

Among other solid tumours, two of 19 patients (10.5%; 95% CI, 1.3–33.1) had objective responses: one with an unspecified BAF47-negative tumour and one with SMARCB1-mutated malignant rhabdoid tumour (response endured for approximately one year). Tumour responses in eight patients with SWI/SNF mutations are summarized in Supplementary Material, Table S8. In addition to the two responders with SMARCB1 alteration/BAF47 loss, an epithelioid angiosarcoma patient had SD, and a patient with malignant tumour of nasal cavity withdrew before evaluation. A patient with ARID1A-mutated endometrial carcinoma achieved PR at week 16 (not confirmed later), with a treatment duration of 7.4 months. Patients with SMARCA4 (n = 2) or BAP1 (n = 1) mutations did not respond (Supplementary Material, Table S8, Figure S3).

The RP2D was determined by integrating clinical safety, PK, PD, and antitumour activity. At 800 mg BID, two of eight evaluable patients had DLTs, 77.8% experienced grade 3–4 TRAEs, and 55.6% required dose interruptions due to TRAEs. PK exposure at 800 mg BID was lower than at 600 mg BID, precluding its use in dose extension. Thus, 400 mg and 600 mg BID were considered for RP2D. Compared with 600 mg BID, 400 mg BID had a better safety profile (lower incidence of grade 3–4 TRAEs and treatment-related SAEs, as well as lower rates of dose reduction, interruption, and discontinuation due to TRAEs). ORR and DCR in patients with ES at 400 mg BID were not less than that at 600 mg BID or even better. Dose-related exposure increase was observed from 50 to 600 mg BID, with dose- and exposure-dependent H3K27me3 inhibition at 200–600 mg BID. Robust inhibition (median >50%) was similar between 400 mg and 600 mg BID, with consistent PK/PD trends in solid tumours. Overall, 400 mg BID showed a more favourable risk–benefit profile and was selected as the RP2D.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This open-label, single-arm, phase I study firstly assessed the safety, PK and PD characteristics of HH2853, a novel EZH1/2 dual inhibitor, in refractory solid tumours and NHLs. The safety profile was acceptable, with the RP2D of 400 mg twice daily. The overall ORR was 29.8% (95% CI, 18.4–43.4), including four CRs. ORR was 31.3% (95% CI, 16.0–50.0) and the median PFS was 16.0 months (5.2–19.1) in patients with ES, indicating that ES represents the potential population for further exploration.

The safety and dose determination were fully assessed in this study. AE spectrum of HH2853 mirrored that of other EZH2 and EZH1/2 inhibitors, such as tazemetostat, SHR2554 and valemetostat.18,26,29 Tazemetostat showed higher risks of asthenia (33–39%), nausea (20–35%) and anaemia (14–16%),21,29 while SHR2554 exhibited a significantly higher incidence of haematological toxicities, including anaemia (41%), white blood count decreased (40%) and platelet count decreased (39%), as well as nausea (21%).18 The incidence of diarrhoea was relative lower in EZH2-selective inhibitors (tazemetostat and SHR2554), Whereas HH2853 (EZH1/EZH2 dual inhibitor) showed higher risks of diarrhoea, anaemia and blood bilirubin increased—side effects less frequently observed with valemetostat.26,27 These can be easily managed by dose interruption and concomitant medication of HH2853. The observed safety differences may reflect the study's unique patient population, which comprised over 80% solid tumour cases compared with valemetostat trials that primarily enrolled patients with NHL. Importantly, the manageable toxicity profile and predictable dose–response relationship support the potential of HH2853 for combination therapies. Current investigations are exploring rational combinations with other targeted agents, leveraging the favourable safety window of HH2853.30,31 The distinct AE profile compared with other inhibitors in its class may inform patient selection and monitoring strategies in future trials, while the demonstrated safety provides a strong foundation for combination regimen development in refractory malignancies.

PK and PD analyses revealed no apparent racial differences and tumour-type differences in HH2853 disposition. The compound demonstrated rapid absorption following oral administration, with a mean elimination half-life supporting twice-daily dosing. Dose-proportional increases in systemic exposure were observed across the 50–600 mg dose range, followed by reduced exposure at 800 mg, suggesting potential absorption saturation at 800 mg despite considerable interpatient variability and limited sample size. Mechanistically, the exposure limitation arises from HH2853's Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS) IV characteristics—high-dose administration (800 mg BID) generates supersaturated solutions that rapidly precipitate, thereby reducing effective drug concentration and systemic exposure.32 PD assessments mirrored these findings, as evidenced by comparable H3K27me3 inhibition between the 400 mg and 600 mg dose levels. The observed plateau in both PK exposure and PD effects above 400 mg further supported this dose selection, as higher doses (600–800 mg) provided no additional PD advantage while potentially increasing toxicity risks. These findings position 400 mg twice daily as an optimal balance between target engagement and clinical tolerability for subsequent development in ES and other relevant indications.

To date, EZH2 inhibitors have demonstrated antitumour activity primarily in NHLs, including FL, adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma and ES.20,25,31 The EZH1/2 dual inhibitor have shown encouraged efficacy in NHLs, but the antitumour activity in ES or other solid tumours remains unclear. In this phase I study of HH2853, over half of objective responses occurred in the patients with ES. And the ORR of HH2853 in patients with ES was 31.3% (95% CI, 16.0–50.0), and the median PFS was 16.0 months (5.2–19.1). The efficacy and survival benefits were to the reported data for tazemetostat, with ORR of 15% and median PFS of 5.5 months.20 This indicates that ES should be the potential population for further exploration. ES is a rare, aggressive subtype of soft-tissue sarcoma characterized by high rates of recurrence, metastasis and mortality with limited treatment options and a poor prognosis.33 Doxorubicin and pazopanib are approved in the US for the treatment of soft tissue sarcoma, with ORRs of 0–22% and median DoRs of less than 2 months.34, 35, 36 Gemcitabine-based therapy also commonly used for ES with ORR of 27–58% and median PFS of 4–8 months as the first-line treatment.34,37 The efficacy in later-line treatment declines sharply, with the ORR of 9–11% and the median PFS of 2.7–6.0 months.35,36,38 This data suggest that HH2853 may represent a novel therapeutic approach and could even be available to challenge the first-line treatment in ES. The loss of BAF47 protein expression is a molecular hallmark of ES.10,39 Dysfunction of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex, including loss-of-function alterations in SMARCB1, SMARCA4, or ARID1A, has been implicated in therapeutic response to HH2853. Notably, solid tumours harbouring these alterations (e.g., SMARCB1-deficient, SMARCA4-mutant, or ARID1A-deficient cancers) are rare and often lack effective treatment options.12,13,40, 41, 42 In this study, three patients with SMARCB1/BAF47-negative/deficient or ARID1A-mutated tumours exhibited clinical benefit from HH2853 treatment. These findings align with previously reported data.43, 44, 45 While the sample size remains limited, these preliminary results tentatively suggest a possible role for HH2853 in certain SWI/SNF-altered solid tumours and further investigation might be warranted.

This study has several limitations. As an open-label, single-arm phase I trial, it was constrained by a small sample size and a limited number of patients within each tumour type, which may introduce selection bias. Additionally, biomarker assessments were conducted using heterogeneous methodologies (e.g., NGS and IHC) across different local laboratories, potentially affecting the accuracy of biomarker analysis and the identification of optimal patient populations for further investigation. Therefore, larger phase II and III studies are warranted to confirm the efficacy of HH2853 in advanced solid tumours, particularly in ES.

In conclusion, HH2853 demonstrated a manageable safety profile and encouraging antitumour activity in refractory solid tumours and NHLs, with particularly promising antitumour activity observed in ES.
